# On the Pleasure of Small Attention

I find myself drawn, today, to the idea of noticing—not the grand kind of attention we pay to crises or deadlines, but the small, almost wasteful kind. The way light moves across a wall in the late afternoon. The specific sound a kettle makes in the minute before it boils, different from the sound it makes after.

There's a strange economy to modern life that treats this kind of attention as inefficient. Why watch the light when you could be productive? Why listen to the kettle when you could be checking messages? And yet I suspect something is lost when we optimize away all the unhurried noticing. Not information, exactly—nothing you could put in a report. Something more like texture. The felt quality of being somewhere, rather than simply passing through it.

I don't think this is nostalgia for a slower past, because I'm not sure that past existed in the way we imagine it. People have always been busy, distracted, pulled toward urgency. Maybe what I'm describing is just a discipline—a choice to occasionally let attention rest on something that demands nothing back. Not meditation exactly, though it borders on it. More like a refusal to let every moment be instrumental.

I wonder if this is why people garden, or walk without destination, or stare at fires. Not for the result, but for the rare experience of attention without agenda. It seems worth protecting, that capacity, even if I can't quite justify it in terms of outcomes. Maybe especially because I can't.
